items.originalTitle: Claude Haiku 5.5
items.summary:
Anthropic has introduced Claude Haiku 5.5, a new AI model designed to be faster and more affordable, matching the price of OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna up to 100,000 tokens but increasing costs beyond that. The model uses a less generous tokenizer, resulting in higher token counts for the same input compared to its predecessor, Haiku 4.5, which was released nearly a year ago at a significantly higher price.

Alongside the model launch, Anthropic has halved the price of cache reads for Sonnet 5.5 and introduced monthly API credits for Max and Team subscribers, ranging from $100 to $500 depending on the plan. These credits match the subscription cost and aim to make API usage more accessible, with options to disable auto-reload to prevent unexpected charges. The credits do not roll over monthly, encouraging users to utilize them within the billing period.

items.originalSummary:
As previously promised, here's Anthropic's new fast, low cost model: Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5.

The previous Haiku, 4.5, was very much showing its age. It came out almost a year ago, and was priced at $1/million input and $5/million output - relatively expensive even back then, and a full 10x the price of OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna, released last month.

The new Haiku exactly matches the price of GPT-6 Luna - $0.10/$0.50 - up to 100,000 tokens. Beyond 100,000 tokens the price increases 5x to $0.50/$2.50. Luna itself has a price increase at 272,000 tokens but only to $0.20/$0.75.

Haiku 5.5 also uses a new, less generous tokenizer. My Claude Token Counter tool shows that the same long prompt uses around 1.25x as many tokens with Haiku 5.5 compared to Haiku 4.5, so there's a hidden price increase there.

If your workloads fit in 100,000 tokens, Haiku is the same price as Luna and reports higher benchmark scores. Above 100,000 tokens, Luna looks like a much better deal.

The most recent release of llm-anthropic finally fixed it so I don't need to ship a new version of that plugin for every new model. I tested the new model like this:

llm install -U llm-anthropic llm anthropic refresh llm -m claude-haiku-5.5 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" -o thinking_effort low

Pelicans

Here are pelicans for low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. The new Haiku doesn't let you disable reasoning, and defaults to medium. I got a good bicycle frame for everything beyond low. The low effort pelican cost 0.0936 cents and took 7 seconds.

This max effort pelican (with a reasoning trace that starts "This is the classic pelican-on-bicycle SVG test...") took 5 minutes 9 seconds to generate, but still only cost me 3.3826 cents:

For comparison, here's the pelican I got a year ago from Haiku 4.5 (for 0.7583 cents - Haiku 4.5 did not support reasoning levels). It sucked at drawing pelicans:

And a generous API credit scheme for subscribers

In addition to Haiku 5.5, Anthropic announced today that they are halving the price of cache reads for Sonnet 5.5. They've also added API credits to subscription plans:

Second, this week, we’ll roll out a new monthly API credit to all Max and Team subscribers for use on the Claude Platform. Max 5x users will get $100 in credits per month, Max 20x users will get $200, and Team subscribers will receive up to $500, pooled across their users.

Claiming this is pleasantly easy: navigate to Settings -> Billing and select the API organization that should benefit from the credits every month:

The API credits exactly match the cost of the subscription itself. This is really generous - it makes it much easier for subscribers to use the API. Anthropic also let you disable auto-reload for the API, with the consequence that "API requests will stop when your balance runs out" - exactly what you want if you're planning to burn through those API credits without risk of a nasty billing surprise.

Note that the monthly credits do not roll over - use them or lose them.

OpenAI still allow you to use your Codex subscription for personal API use, which works out as a better deal for heavy API users. This new credit scheme goes at least some way to overcoming that difference.

items.title: Michael Lynch outlines common anti-patterns in software blogging, warning against meandering intros, overreliance on links, and excessive formality
items.originalTitle: Anti-Patterns in Software Blogging
items.summary: Michael Lynch offers advice on software blogging pitfalls, cautioning writers against lengthy introductions, assuming readers' prior knowledge, and relying too much on links instead of explaining terms. He emphasizes that articles should be understandable even without clicking external links. Lynch also encourages bloggers to write in a natural, conversational style rather than a stiff, formal tone, noting that many developers delegating writing to AI have made software blogging bland and uniform, while readers seek more personality in writing.

items.originalSummary:
Anti-Patterns in Software Blogging

Some excellent writing advice from Michael Lynch. Michael warns against "meandering intros", misjudging your reader's existing knowledge, assuming they'll read your previous posts, and excessive formality.

He also warns against overreliance on links as an excuse not to explain terminology. This one hurt! I do this all the time, but I have a nagging suspicion that almost nobody ever clicks on them.

(In a Lobste.rs comment Michael clarifies that "My rule of thumb is that my article should still make sense to the reader even if they don't click any links". That works for me.)

This point about using your own voice is crucial:

Beginner software bloggers suffer from a mass delusion that you have to write in a stiff, overly formal way for people to take you seriously [...]

Just write the way you talk.

With so many developers delegating their writing to AI, software blogging is becoming bland and homogenous. Readers are hungry for writing with personality.

Via Lobste.rs

items.title: Meta and Microsoft reduce employee use of Anthropic’s Claude AI as they shift to proprietary coding tools [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Meta and Microsoft take steps to reduce employee usage of Claude AI
items.summary:
Meta and Microsoft have started limiting their employees' use of Anthropic's Claude AI, focusing instead on their own AI coding assistants. This move aims to control internal AI spending and streamline development processes without affecting customer access to Claude through Microsoft’s platforms.

Microsoft has cut internal AI spending limits significantly, reducing monthly allowances from $100,000 to about $10,000 per employee in many cases, while Meta’s Claude Code users dropped from around 60,000 to 30,000 amid a shift to MetaCode and Muse Code, its proprietary AI tools. Despite fewer users, Meta’s spending on Claude remains substantial, reflecting ongoing demand and competition in AI development.

The transition highlights the challenges of managing AI costs and security risks, as vulnerabilities in AI coding assistants have been identified and addressed. Both companies continue to invest in AI but are tightening budgets and prioritizing their own technologies amid a competitive landscape.

items.title: Researchers show AI autoformalisation in Lean may misrepresent natural language proofs, including OpenAI's Navier-Stokes blow-up claim [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Navier–Stokes Lost in Translation
items.summary: A new study demonstrates that translating mathematical proofs from natural language into formal languages like Lean using AI does not guarantee the original argument's correctness. The researchers highlight that resolving ambiguities in mathematical language is computationally more complex than any known problem, including the Halting problem, making faithful AI autoformalisation effectively impossible. They provide examples where AI mistranslations led to discrepancies between natural language proofs and their formal verifications, specifically pointing out that OpenAI's announced proof of blow-up solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations does not correspond accurately between the natural language and Lean formalisation.

items.title: Docker launches Docker Agent CLI plugin for building and running AI agents with YAML configs and multi-agent orchestration [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Docker Agent
items.summary:
Docker Agent is a new CLI plugin that enables users to create, run, and share AI agents defined in declarative YAML configurations without coding. It supports multi-agent collaboration, integrates with various AI providers including OpenAI and Anthropic, and offers a rich ecosystem of tools and retrieval-augmented generation features.

The plugin is pre-installed with Docker Desktop 4.63+ and can also be installed via Homebrew or binary releases. Users can run agents locally or from OCI registries, and the system supports both cloud API keys and local models through Docker Model Runner. Docker collects anonymous telemetry data to improve the tool and maintains community support through Docker Community Slack channels.

items.originalTitle: Sharing AI progress in mathematics
items.summary:
OpenAI has released a collection of new mathematical findings generated by an internal frontier AI model, sharing formalized proofs in the Lean programming language and detailed research data on GitHub. The release follows consultations with the Institute for Advanced Study's Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence to establish best practices for sharing AI-generated mathematical work.

The GitHub repository includes protocols for paper revisions, citations, and summaries of the model's reasoning, along with compute usage estimates equivalent to about three hours of ChatGPT Pro per result. OpenAI plans to fund workshops and programs to further explore AI-produced mathematical results and aims to responsibly release the model while continuing to refine standards based on community feedback.

Despite Smith's legal team's request for probation, the court emphasized the need for deterrence against such sophisticated fraud schemes.

items.summary:
Law firms have not seen a decline in legal billing rates or hours worked despite adopting AI tools, as increased demand and the need to review AI-generated work maintain or raise workloads. Most legal spending remains hourly, and many in-house lawyers report no significant cost savings from AI use. Firms are investing heavily in AI platforms but face challenges in adjusting compensation models tied to billable hours.

The persistence of high billing rates and hours is attributed to factors such as increased work volume, more extensive diligence requirements, and additional review time for AI outputs. Some clients forbid AI-generated deliverables, complicating cost reductions. Ethical guidelines require lawyers to bill only actual time spent, limiting the ability to pass AI tool costs to clients without disclosure. Firms are experimenting with fixed fees and tracking AI usage to adapt to these changes.

This dynamic creates tension between efficiency gains from AI and traditional legal billing practices, with firms cautious about reducing fees despite technological advances. The evolving landscape raises questions about future billing models and client expectations as AI becomes more integrated into legal workflows.

However, experts caution that AI's benefits come with risks, emphasizing the need for balanced data access, privacy, regulation, and capacity building to ensure equitable and effective use. Successful AI integration in food systems will require collaboration among technical developers, policymakers, and local stakeholders to create community-specific solutions and avoid repeating past agricultural pitfalls.

items.summary:

Databricks and Stripe had already been talking to the startup about a potential sale. Nvidia was late to the party. The chipmaker’s CEO, Jensen Huang, wanted in.

Nvidia executives told their counterparts at OpenRouter they were interested and were prepared to make a generous offer, but they needed more time to evaluate a possible transaction before doing so, said a person with knowledge of the discussion. OpenRouter’s founders didn’t want to wait. Ultimately, Nvidia—whose interest in the startup hasn’t previously been reported—didn’t make a formal offer, and Stripe prevailed with an $8 billion bid for OpenRouter.

Nvidia’s dealmakers quickly moved on to other prizes. Over the next two months, they inked more than $140 billion worth of deals—including a $105 billion credit guarantee. The company held nearly $100 billion worth of equity investments and $25 billion in future investment commitments as of late July. More deals are likely.

items.title: AI Agenda Live: From Token Maxing to Value maxing: Getting More From Every Unit of Compute [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI Agenda Live: From Token Maxing to Value maxing: Getting More From Every Unit of Compute
items.summary:
In AI circles, conversations about compute shortages are as common as talk of the weather. As agentic workflows threaten to multiply token consumption further, it’s little wonder that talk has shifted from securing GPUs to optimizing them.

At a recent panel, The Information’s Phoebe Liu sat down with three AI leaders—from chipmakers and AI clouds to Fortune 500s—to discuss how they’re squeezing more tokens from every unit of compute. Those on the panel were:

  • Marc Boroditsky, Chief Revenue Officer, Nebius
  • Mattie Toia, VP, Infrastructure, Uber
  • Dion Harris, Sr. Director, HPC & AI Hyperscale Infrastructure Solutions, NVIDIA

Optimizing to the customer’s KPI

Nebius was recently rated Platinum, the top tier, in SemiAnalysis’ ClusterMAX rating, which puts GPU cloud providers through a suite of hands-on tests on the compute they supply. This distinction, said Chief Revenue Officer Marc Boroditsky, reflects the company’s ability to deliver high performance at high efficiency.

“Not only are we a well-regarded supplier for neolabs, but we’re also enterprise-grade, so ready to supply the entire market,” he said.

He noted that Nebius tailors optimizations in Nebius Token Factory, its inference platform, to specific customer’s specific goals, whether speed, reliability, quality or price.

One recent example of how they do this is speculative decoding, which allows smaller models to predict likely next tokens that a larger model verifies in bulk, rather than generating one token at a time. Nebius uses each customer’s own traffic to improve the result.

NVIDIA, meanwhile, is helping companies avoid unnecessary compute altogether. A feature in its Dynamo platform locates already-computed data sitting in a cluster’s KV cache so teams don’t waste compute recalculating it.

“We’re seeing a lot of bang for the buck in terms of driving performance, efficiency and overall effectiveness,” noted NVIDIA’s Dion Harris.

Uber has seen its token costs stabilize in recent months even as its use of agentic workflows has grown, said Mattie Toia. She credited caching pushed down to individual sub-agents, plus a simpler shift: giving engineers visibility into their own usage.

“It starts by giving visibility to individual users—how many tokens they’re spending, the relative cost of them. That gives people context to think about how they’re optimizing,” she said.

Boroditsky described the shift as moving from “token maxing” to “value maxing”: measuring how many agent turns, tokens and dollars it takes to reach an outcome, whether that’s a document or a completed form.

“What you’re looking for is, how do I actually optimize the value that I’m creating for the cost that I’m spending?” he said.

The ecosystem at work

Improving the economics of compute is a job for the whole industry, not any one company, the panel agreed. “It takes a lot more than a chip to deliver AI at scale,” Harris said.

He pointed to compounding gains from pairing new hardware with better software—kernel tuning, smarter frameworks, and tools built across NVIDIA’s ecosystem. Over a chip’s lifetime, this can drive 3-5X performance gains from day zero to year five.

Boroditsky added that no single model wins every use case.

“Models matter a lot, but by themselves, they don’t solve a problem,” he said. “It’s the entire end-to-end solution.”

Data discipline

One thing companies can do today, Toia said, is get their own data in order.

“There is a lot of valuable data that most organizations have that is really important to grounding your models,” she said. Uber built an internal “context graph”—roughly 24 million nodes pulled from Jira tickets, system design docs and code reviews—to feed its AI agents better context, cutting query times from 20 minutes to 30 seconds while using fewer tokens.

Boroditsky agreed with this approach, noting that the companies that build centralized resources get better results. His five-year prediction: “The leading companies in the market will have taken control of their intelligence.”

The future of pricing

Asked whether Nebius would consider outcome-based pricing, Boroditsky said the company was open to the idea.

“I don’t think we’ve figured out yet the right economic model between the supplier and the customer,” he said.

Nebius already runs capacity auctions and recently launched spot pricing. As the applications built on Nebius move toward outcome-based models, Boroditsky noted that vendors will have to adapt. Looking ahead, he expects managed services to route workloads intelligently on customers’ behalf.

“In the coming quarters, you’re going to see a lot more managed services that are doing more of the heavy lifting,” he said.
